definition: Individuals aged 13 to 18 years undergoing puberty and adolescent development, with distinct biological vulnerabilities and behavioural risk profiles compared to younger children and adults.
Adults aged 19 to 44 years, typically characterised by peak physical capacity, reproductive activity, and workforce participation.
Older adults aged 65 to 78 years, often retaining significant functional capacity but with increasing chronic disease burden and growing vulnerability to environmental stressors.
Individuals aged 80 years and older, the fastest-growing demographic in many populations, with the highest prevalence of frailty, multimorbidity, and vulnerability to adverse health events.
Individuals aged 65 years and older, a broad group encompassing younger-old and oldest-old adults with increasing prevalence of chronic disease, frailty, and functional decline.
Adults aged 45 to 64 years, a life stage associated with the onset of chronic non-communicable diseases and changing physiological risk profiles.
Individuals aged 19 years and older, encompassing young adults, middle-aged, and older adult sub-groups across the adult life course.
Studies or data that encompass individuals across all age groups without restriction, or where findings apply across the full life course.
Children aged 6 to 12 years in middle childhood, a period of continued physical growth, cognitive development, and increasing social independence.
Children aged 2 to 5 years in the preschool developmental stage, characterised by rapid brain development, high activity levels, and reliance on caregivers for protection from environmental hazards.
Children aged 2 to 12 years, spanning early childhood through to pre-adolescence, during which physical, cognitive, and social development are particularly sensitive to environmental conditions.
Infants in the first 28 days of life, a critical period of physiological adaptation with high vulnerability to infection, thermal stress, and nutritional insufficiency.
Children aged 1 to 23 months, a developmental period of rapid growth, nutritional dependency, and heightened susceptibility to infectious disease and environmental exposures.
Studies or data that include individuals of all gender identities or both sexes without stratification, or where findings apply across the full gender spectrum.
Individuals whose gender identity or expression differs from the sex assigned at birth, including transgender, non-binary, and other gender-diverse people.
Individuals identified as female by biological sex or gender identity, used to stratify health data or describe sex-specific biological and social health determinants.
Individuals identified as male by biological sex or gender identity, used to stratify health data or describe sex-specific biological and social health determinants.
Individuals living with one or more long-term physical health conditions that reduce physiological resilience and increase susceptibility to adverse health outcomes.

Individuals with physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairments that limit daily functioning and may increase exposure to harm and reduce capacity to respond to environmental or social stressors.
Population groups defined by shared ethnic, cultural, or racial identity that may face structural disadvantage, discrimination, or disproportionate exposure to environmental and social risk factors.
Older adults with reduced physiological reserve and resilience, characterised by weakness, fatigue, and vulnerability to adverse health outcomes following minor stressors.
Populations with historical, cultural, and territorial ties to lands prior to colonisation, who often face compounded social, economic, and environmental vulnerabilities.
Young children and infants whose immature physiological systems, developmental dependency, and limited autonomy increase their susceptibility to environmental exposures and health harms.

Individuals and households with insufficient financial resources to meet basic needs, facing compounded vulnerability through reduced access to healthcare, nutrition, safe housing, and adaptive capacity.
People who have moved within or across borders, voluntarily or under duress, and who may face elevated health risks due to displacement, poor living conditions, and restricted access to services.

Individuals whose occupation exposes them to elevated health hazards, including outdoor workers in agriculture, construction, and other sectors with high physical exposure to environmental conditions.

Individuals during pregnancy, whose altered physiology and increased metabolic demands heighten susceptibility to environmental exposures and infectious disease with potential consequences for both maternal and foetal health.
Women as a population group who may face heightened vulnerability due to biological factors, gender-based inequalities in resource access, and higher exposure to specific social and economic risks.
A peer-reviewed research output published in an academic journal, including full research articles, letters to the editor, commentaries, and opinion pieces.
Reports published outside the classic editorial route, predominantly by intergovernmental organizations, supra-national organizations, NGOs, governments.
A registered or published research protocol or trials registry record describing a study that is planned or underway but has not yet reported results.
A research manuscript that has been made publicly available prior to formal peer review and journal publication, such as those posted on medRxiv or SSRN.
A detailed account of a single individual's or unit's exposure, condition, and outcome, used to generate hypotheses or describe novel or rare phenomena.
A descriptive report of characteristics and outcomes among a series of individuals sharing a common exposure or condition, without a control group.
A study design that collects data from a population at a single point in time, describing the prevalence of exposures and outcomes without follow-up.
Study designs that describe characteristics, frequency, or distribution of outcomes in a single group without a comparison group or temporal manipulation.

A quasi-experimental method comparing the change in outcomes over time between a group exposed to an intervention and an unexposed control group, to estimate causal effects under the parallel trends assumption.

A method estimating the effect of an event or intervention by examining outcome trends relative to the timing of the event, often used to test pre-treatment parallel trends and assess dynamic treatment effects.

A regression approach using repeated observations on the same units over time to control for time-invariant unobserved confounding, including standard fixed effects, panel regression, and adjusted cohort analysis.
A quasi-experimental method using a variable that affects exposure but not the outcome directly (an instrument) to estimate causal effects in the presence of unmeasured confounding.
A method pairing treated and untreated units on observed characteristics or estimated propensity scores to construct a balanced comparison group and reduce confounding bias.
A quasi-experimental design exploiting a threshold in a continuous assignment variable to estimate causal effects for units just above and below the cutoff, where assignment is effectively random.
A quasi-experimental method constructing a weighted combination of untreated units to serve as a counterfactual for a treated unit, used when only a small number of aggregate units are available.

An experimental or quasi-experimental study in which participants are allocated to intervention and comparison groups through a process other than randomisation, using statistical methods to control for confounding.

A study in which allocation to intervention and control conditions occurs through a process that approximates randomisation but is not under the investigator's full control, such as policy roll-out or natural variation.
An experimental or quasi-experimental study in which the method of allocation to groups is not clearly reported, precluding classification as randomised or non-randomised.
An experimental study in which participants are randomly allocated to intervention or control groups, considered the gold standard for evaluating causal effects of interventions.
Experimental study designs that compare outcomes between an intervention group and one or more control or comparison groups, with or without randomisation.

pref_label: Single arm trial / single arm experiment
definition: An experimental study in which all participants receive the intervention and outcomes are compared to a pre-specified target or historical baseline, without a concurrent control arm.
Experimental study designs in which an intervention is applied to a single group without a concurrent control group, limiting but not eliminating causal inference.
A macroeconomic modelling approach representing interactions across sectors of an economy to estimate the economy-wide effects of policy changes, including those with health implications.

pref_label: Integrated assessment model (IAM) / health impact projection
definition: A modelling approach linking climate, economic, and social systems to project future health impacts under different emissions or policy scenarios, often at national or global scale.
A modelling approach simulating the behaviour and outcomes of individual units — people, households, or firms — over time to estimate aggregate population-level effects of policies or exposures.

Climate or environmental modelling and simulation approaches not classified under IAM, CGE, or microsimulation, including downscaled climate models, exposure models, and environmental simulation tools.
Health modelling and simulation approaches not classified under IAM, CGE, or microsimulation, including epidemiological models, disease transmission models, and burden of disease projections.
Study designs using mathematical, statistical, or computational models to simulate real-world systems, project future outcomes, or estimate impacts under defined scenarios.

A time series analysis comparing outcome trends before and after an intervention or exposure in both an intervention group and a concurrent control group, strengthening causal inference over uncontrolled ITS.
A study that retrospectively compares individuals with a health outcome (cases) to those without (controls) to identify differences in prior exposure, often using matching to reduce confounding.
A study that follows a defined group of individuals over time, measuring exposures and outcomes prospectively or retrospectively to assess associations and temporal relationships.

A study comparing pre- and post-intervention outcomes in both an intervention group and a non-randomised control group, improving on uncontrolled before-after designs by accounting for secular trends.
Observational study designs that compare health outcomes between two or more groups defined by exposure status, without random allocation.
A time series analysis of outcome data at multiple time points before and after an intervention or exposure in a single group, without a control series to account for concurrent trends.
A study that compares outcomes measured in the same group before and after an exposure or intervention, without a concurrent control group.
Observational study designs that track outcomes over time in a single group without a concurrent comparison group, relying on temporal patterns to infer associations.
A qualitative research design using immersive fieldwork, participant observation, or in-depth interviews to explore lived experiences, cultural practices, and social contexts.
A qualitative method collecting data through facilitated group discussion among selected participants, used to explore shared perspectives, norms, and experiences on a defined topic.
A research design that integrates quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis within a single study, combining the strengths of both approaches to address research questions.
Study designs using qualitative data collection and analysis, or combining qualitative and quantitative approaches, to explore meanings, experiences, and contextual factors.
Primary research study designs not captured by the specific categories of descriptive, observational, experimental, qualitative, or modelling designs.
Original research studies that collect and analyse data directly, as distinct from evidence syntheses that aggregate findings from existing studies.

A systematically developed statement providing recommendations to guide clinical or public health practice, typically based on a synthesis of the available evidence. Often with systematic methods, but sometimes also based on expert consensus.
A comprehensive policy-relevant evaluation of a health technology that typically includes clinical effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and broader social and ethical considerations.
A non-systematic review that summarises and interprets the literature on a topic based on the author's expertise and judgement, without exhaustive or reproducible search methods.
A systematic mapping exercise that visually represents the distribution of evidence across a framework of interventions and outcomes, highlighting areas where evidence is absent or weak.
A systematic review conducted with comprehensive search strategies and full methodological rigour, without time or resource constraints that would limit its scope.

A systematic review that integrates findings from both quantitative and qualitative primary studies, using mixed-methods synthesis approaches to address questions that neither approach could answer alone.
A systematic review that searches for, appraises, and synthesises findings from qualitative primary studies, using methods such as meta-ethnography, thematic synthesis, or framework synthesis.
A systematic review conducted within a shortened timeframe using streamlined methods, trading some comprehensiveness for speed to meet urgent policy or practice needs.

A theory-driven review methodology that explores how and why interventions work in particular contexts and for whom, generating or testing explanatory theories rather than aggregating effect estimates.
A systematic review that maps the extent, range, and nature of evidence on a broad topic without synthesising findings, used to identify gaps and inform future research priorities.
A review that uses explicit, reproducible methods to systematically search, select, appraise, and synthesise evidence from primary studies on a defined research question.
A synthesis that systematically compiles and summarises findings from multiple systematic reviews on a related topic, providing a high-level overview of the evidence base.
Evidence synthesis types not captured by the specific categories of systematic review, umbrella review, narrative review, guideline, or health technology assessment.
Research that systematically or narratively aggregates and synthesises findings from multiple primary studies to draw broader conclusions about a topic.

Adaptation actions that inadvertently increase vulnerability or exposure to harm, reduce adaptive capacity, or create new risks for human or natural systems, often as an unintended consequence of well-intentioned interventions.
Adjustments in natural or human systems in response to actual or anticipated climate change, intended to moderate harm or exploit beneficial opportunities arising from climate variability.
The process of establishing the causal contribution of climate change to observed changes in physical, ecological, or human systems, including specific extreme weather events or health outcomes.
Projected effects on human health, ecosystems, and societies arising from anticipated changes in climate over coming decades, typically derived from climate modelling and scenario analysis.
Negative consequences of climate change that cannot be avoided through mitigation or adaptation, including irreversible harm to lives, livelihoods, cultural heritage, ecosystems, and infrastructure.
The effects of climate change on natural and human systems, including consequences for health, ecosystems, economies, and societies resulting from climate variability and change.

Positive health, social, or environmental benefits arising from mitigation actions that are additional to the primary goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions, such as improved air quality or increased physical activity.
Actions and strategies aimed at reducing or preventing greenhouse gas emissions in order to limit the magnitude of future climate change and its associated health and environmental impacts.

scheme_name: E.1 Climate factors - Climate drivers / variability
definition: General changes in weather patterns not attributed to a specific meteorological variable, used when studies refer to weather variability in broad terms.

scheme_name: E.1 Climate factors - Climate drivers / variability
definition: Climate change where the specific driver or mechanism is not identified or distinguished, used when studies refer to climate change in general terms.

scheme_name: E.1 Climate factors - Climate drivers / variability
definition: Accelerated melting of glaciers and snowpack due to rising temperatures, affecting freshwater supply, sea levels, and downstream ecosystems.

scheme_name: E.1 Climate factors - Climate drivers / variability
definition: Shifts in atmospheric moisture levels that affect thermal comfort, respiratory health, and the prevalence of moisture-related diseases.

scheme_name: E.1 Climate factors - Climate drivers / variability
definition: Alterations in the amount, timing, or intensity of rainfall and snowfall, affecting water availability, flood risk, and drought conditions.

scheme_name: E.1 Climate factors - Climate drivers / variability
definition: The increase in mean sea level resulting from thermal expansion of seawater and melting ice, threatening coastal communities, infrastructure, and freshwater resources.

scheme_name: E.1 Climate factors - Climate drivers / variability
definition: Shifts in the duration of seasons, including earlier spring onset and extended summers, with consequences for agriculture, vector biology, and human health.

scheme_name: E.1 Climate factors - Climate drivers / variability
definition: Long-term shifts in average or extreme temperature conditions, including warming trends, that affect human health, ecosystems, and society.

scheme_name: E.1 Climate factors - Climate drivers / variability
definition: Alterations in wind patterns and velocity that can affect air quality, energy systems, and the spread of airborne pathogens and pollutants.

scheme_name: E.1 Climate factors - Climate drivers / variability
definition: Climate variability refers to fluctuations in climate conditions (temperature, precipitation, wind patterns, etc.) over months, years, or decades around a longer-term average. Climate variability is influenced by multiple climate drivers.

scheme_name: E.2 Climate factors - Extreme weather events
definition: Extreme weather events where the specific type is not identified, used when studies refer to climate extremes without distinguishing between event types.

scheme_name: E.2 Climate factors - Extreme weather events
definition: Prolonged periods of abnormally low rainfall leading to water scarcity, crop failure, and increased risk of wildfires, with significant health and livelihood consequences.

scheme_name: E.2 Climate factors - Extreme weather events
definition: Episodes of abnormally low temperatures, including cold snaps and blizzards, associated with increased risk of hypothermia, cardiovascular events, and respiratory illness.

scheme_name: E.2 Climate factors - Extreme weather events
definition: Periods of abnormally high temperatures, including heatwaves, that pose direct health risks such as heat exhaustion, heat stroke, and excess mortality.

scheme_name: E.2 Climate factors - Extreme weather events
definition: Temporary inundation of normally dry land caused by excessive rainfall, storm surges, or rapid snowmelt, posing risks to human health, displacement, and infrastructure.

scheme_name: E.2 Climate factors - Extreme weather events
definition: Intense meteorological events including tropical cyclones, hurricanes, typhoons, and severe thunderstorms, causing wind damage, flooding, and displacement.

scheme_name: E.2 Climate factors - Extreme weather events
definition: Uncontrolled fires in natural vegetation, increasingly associated with drought and heat, producing smoke and air pollution with severe respiratory and cardiovascular health impacts.

scheme_name: E.3 Climate factors - Climate forcing agents
definition: Atmospheric gases that trap heat and contribute to the greenhouse effect, referred to collectively without specifying the individual gas type.

scheme_name: E.3 Climate factors - Climate forcing agents
definition: The primary long-lived greenhouse gas produced by fossil fuel combustion, deforestation, and industrial processes, responsible for the majority of anthropogenic radiative forcing.

scheme_name: E.3 Climate factors - Climate forcing agents
pref_label: Fluorinated gases / hydrofluorocarbons / perfluorocarbons / sulfur hexafluoride / nitrogen trifluoride
definition: A group of potent synthetic greenhouse gases used in industrial applications, refrigeration, and electronics manufacturing, with very high global warming potentials and long atmospheric lifetimes.

scheme_name: E.3 Climate factors - Climate forcing agents
definition: A potent short-lived greenhouse gas emitted from livestock, rice cultivation, landfills, and fossil fuel extraction, with a global warming potential far exceeding that of CO₂ over 20 years.

scheme_name: E.3 Climate factors - Climate forcing agents
definition: A greenhouse gas and ozone-depleting substance emitted primarily from agricultural soils, livestock, and nitrogen fertilisers, with a high global warming potential.

scheme_name: E.3 Climate factors - Climate forcing agents
pref_label: Ozone-depleting substances / chlorofluorocarbons / hydrochlorofluorocarbons / halons / carbon tetrachloride / methyl chloroform
definition: Chemical compounds that destroy stratospheric ozone and act as potent greenhouse gases, regulated under the Montreal Protocol due to their combined climate and health impacts.

scheme_name: E.3 Climate factors - Climate forcing agents
pref_label: Particulate matter (PM10) / fine particulate matter (PM2.5) / black/organic carbon / sulfate/nitrate aerosols
definition: Airborne particles of 10 or 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter. Fine particulate matter can include components such as black carbon and sulfate aerosols, that affect both climate and human health through respiratory and cardiovascular pathways.

scheme_name: E.3 Climate factors - Climate forcing agents
definition: A short-lived climate pollutant and air quality hazard formed by photochemical reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, harmful to respiratory health.
Fossil fuel use or combustion where the specific fuel type is not identified, used when studies refer to fossil fuels in general without distinguishing between coal, oil, or gas.
A solid fossil fuel formed from ancient plant matter, the most carbon-intensive energy source and a major contributor to greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution.
A fossil fuel composed primarily of methane, used for heating, electricity generation, and industrial processes, with lower CO₂ emissions than coal but significant methane leakage risks.
A liquid fossil fuel refined into petroleum products including petrol, diesel, and jet fuel, a major source of greenhouse gas emissions from transport and industry.
Participation in collective and political processes aimed at influencing climate policy, community resilience planning, or social responses to climate hazards.
Actions taken at the household level to reduce exposure to hazards or improve living conditions, such as installing insulation, flood barriers, ventilation, or emergency preparedness measures.
Acquiring knowledge and skills that enable individuals and communities to understand risks, make informed decisions, and adapt their behaviours and livelihoods accordingly.
Changes to daily routines, work patterns, or living arrangements made within a person's current location in response to changing conditions, without relocating.
Movement of individuals or communities away from areas made uninhabitable or highly hazardous by climate change, including both voluntary relocation and forced displacement.
Adaptation behaviours not classified under the specific categories of civic engagement, psychological coping, household protection, learning, lifestyle change in place, migration, or self-protection.
Psychological strategies and mental health practices that individuals use to manage stress, anxiety, and trauma associated with climate change and climate-related disasters.
Individual actions taken to protect personal health from climate hazards, such as using sunscreen, staying hydrated during heat events, or wearing respiratory protection during wildfires.
Deliberate actions taken by individuals or communities to reduce exposure or vulnerability to climate-related hazards and protect health and livelihoods.

Changes in dietary patterns and food purchasing behaviour, such as reducing meat intake, minimising food waste, or choosing locally produced food, to lower the environmental footprint of food consumption.

Reductions or shifts in the purchase and use of physical goods and services to lower associated environmental impacts, including buying less, repairing, reusing, or choosing lower-impact products and services.

Actions taken at the household level to reduce energy consumption and associated emissions, including reducing heating and cooling use, improving insulation, and adopting lower-emission energy sources.
Behavioural changes in how individuals travel and commute, such as switching to public transport, cycling, walking, or reducing vehicle use, to reduce transport-related emissions.
Mitigation behaviours not classified under the specific categories of mobility, household, food and diet, or goods and consumption.
Voluntary or encouraged changes in individual and household behaviour that reduce greenhouse gas emissions across key consumption domains.
Human behaviours, social practices, and cultural norms that influence greenhouse gas emissions or shape vulnerability and resilience to climate change impacts.
Locally designed and led responses to climate-health risks, drawing on community knowledge and priorities to develop contextually appropriate adaptation strategies.

Culturally grounded practices, knowledge systems, and identities that support individual and community wellbeing, including indigenous-led approaches and the preservation of connections to land and heritage.
The legal and customary rights of communities and indigenous peoples to access, use, and govern land and natural resources, underpinning livelihood security and self-determination.
Processes that involve communities in decision-making and planning, ensuring local voices shape policies, programmes, and strategies that affect them.
Community networks and informal support systems that enable mutual assistance during times of stress or shock, including food sharing, community care, and grassroots first response.
Community-based interventions not classified under community-based adaptation, participatory governance, social cohesion, cultural identity, or land and resource rights.
Locally designed and led interventions that mobilise communities to address climate-health risks, drawing on local knowledge, social networks, and collective action.

Conservation and restoration of coastal and marine ecosystems including mangroves, coral reefs, and wetlands, providing storm surge protection, food security, flood buffering, and wellbeing co-benefits.

Sustainable management and restoration of forests and land, including wildfire prevention, reforestation, agroforestry, peatland restoration for biodiversity and carbon sequestration, regenerative agriculture for soil health and food security, and ecological approaches to reducing disease vector habitat.
Parks, street trees, green corridors, and urban water bodies that reduce heat island effects, support mental health, and increase urban resilience through ecosystem services.
Ecosystem-based interventions not classified under urban green-blue infrastructure, coastal and marine protection, or forest and land management.

Interventions that use the sustainable management, conservation, or restoration of ecosystems to reduce climate-related health risks and deliver co-benefits for biodiversity and human wellbeing, including urban green-blue infrastructure, coastal and marine protection, and forest and land management.
Systems and institutions for preparedness, response, and recovery in relation to emergencies and disasters, including early warning, evacuation planning, and surge capacity for acute events.

Institutional actions to design and strengthen health systems for climate resilience, including decentralisation, workforce and capacity building in climate-sensitive disease, updating clinical guidelines for climate risks, and ensuring flood, heat, and storm resilience of health facilities and supply chains.
International funding, technical assistance, and development programmes directed at lower-income countries to support economic development, institutional capacity, and service delivery.

Research infrastructure, knowledge translation systems, and educational programmes that build understanding of risks and promote evidence-informed decision-making and behaviour change at individual or community level.
Institutional interventions not classified under health system governance, research and education, emergency management, or international development and aid.

Actions taken by formal organisations and institutions — including governments, health systems, and international bodies — to build climate resilience and coordinate adaptation or mitigation efforts, spanning health system governance, research and education, emergency management, and international development.
Market-based and fiscal mechanisms such as carbon taxes, emissions trading schemes, and subsidies used to incentivise emissions reductions or climate adaptation investments.

A governance approach that systematically integrates health considerations into climate policy and climate considerations into health policy, recognising that health outcomes are shaped by decisions made across multiple sectors including energy, transport, food, and land use.

Formal binding or non-binding agreements between nations or organisations to coordinate action on climate change, including treaties, protocols, and multilateral accords, e.g. UNFCCC mechanisms, Paris Agreement, WHO frameworks.

Institutional frameworks, strategies, and targets that guide governments and organisations in planning and implementing climate action, including national determined contributions, national adaptation plans and climate plans (e.g. land use policy, city-level climate health strategies, spatial planning, urban heat island reduction, flood plain management), surveillance and early-warning policy (mandated disease surveillance, heat alert systems), climate-change related public health information and education.

Legally binding rules, standards, and enforcement mechanisms that mandate emissions reductions, land use changes, or other climate-related behaviours by governments, industries, or individuals. E.g. emissions standards, environmental health regulations, fossil fuel bans.
Formal rules, regulations, and governance instruments designed by governments or international bodies to drive climate mitigation, adaptation, or resilience-building.

Built environment designs and retrofits that reduce heat exposure and improve thermal comfort, including cool roofs, reflective surfaces, passive cooling design, and heat-resilient housing construction.

Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure designed to remain functional under changing precipitation patterns, including flood-proof and drought-resilient water supply systems and sanitation systems adapted to climate variability.

Physical infrastructure protecting coastal and flood-prone communities from climate-related inundation, including sea walls, improved drainage systems, and managed retreat programmes that reduce population exposure.

Digital tools and data infrastructure supporting climate-health surveillance and response, including remote sensing, climate-health surveillance platforms, vector surveillance systems, and early warning and forecasting systems for climate-sensitive health risks.
Technologies that maintain food availability and safety under a changing climate, including drought-resistant crop varieties and cold chain systems that preserve food safety under warming conditions.
Adaptation technologies and infrastructure not classified under the specific categories of water and sanitation, built environment, digital systems, food security, or coastal and flood defence.
Technologies and built infrastructure designed to reduce vulnerability to climate impacts, including flood defences, heat-resilient buildings, and early warning systems.
Buildings with poor insulation or energy performance that rely on fossil fuel heating and cooling systems, contributing to both emissions and energy poverty.
Power generation infrastructure using coal, oil, or gas combustion, associated with significant greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution health burdens.
Agricultural systems with high greenhouse gas footprints, including intensive livestock operations, synthetic fertiliser supply chains, and irrigation systems with large energy demands.
Mining, cement, steel, chemical, and other extractive and heavy industrial processes associated with high greenhouse gas emissions and direct health burdens from air, water, and soil pollution.
Road networks and vehicle fleets designed around internal combustion engines, generating traffic-related air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions with well-documented health impacts.
Waste disposal systems including landfills and open burning that generate methane and toxic air pollutants, contributing to both climate forcing and direct health harm.
Emitting technologies and infrastructure not classified under the specific categories of energy, transport, agriculture, built environment, industrial, or waste systems.
Technologies and infrastructure that generate significant greenhouse gas emissions, whose phase-out or retrofitting is central to climate mitigation strategies. Covers so-called brown technologies.
Engineered systems that capture CO₂ from point sources or directly from the atmosphere and store it permanently, including carbon capture and storage (CCS) and direct air capture technologies.

Technologies and infrastructure for producing and distributing energy from low- or zero-carbon sources, including renewable energy systems, household energy access, cookstove replacement reducing indoor air pollution and emissions, and smart grid optimisation.

Technologies and infrastructure that reduce energy consumption, including energy-efficient appliances, green buildings, housing insulation, and retrofits that reduce heating and cooling energy demand.
Infrastructure and systems enabling low-emission travel and transport, including active travel networks, electric vehicle charging infrastructure, and public transit systems.
Low-emission agricultural technologies and food production systems, including plant-based food production, sustainable land management, and infrastructure for reducing food loss and waste.
Sanitation and waste management systems that reduce methane emissions and disease vectors, including circular economy approaches that minimise waste generation and improve resource recovery.
Mitigation technologies and infrastructure not classified under the specific categories of clean energy, transport, energy efficiency, food systems, waste management, or carbon capture.
Technologies and infrastructure designed to reduce or eliminate greenhouse gas emissions.

Physical systems, equipment, and built infrastructure deployed to address environmental, social, or economic challenges, including systems designed to reduce emissions, improve resilience, or support service delivery.
The sector encompassing crop cultivation, livestock rearing, aquaculture, fishing, and forest management.
The sector covering residential and commercial buildings, housing provision, and construction.
The sector encompassing formal and informal education systems, including schools, universities, and vocational institutions.
The sector covering electricity generation, fuel production, and resource extraction, including both fossil fuel and renewable energy systems.
The sector encompassing banking, insurance, investment, and financial services, including public and private finance mechanisms.
The sector providing medical care, public health services, and health infrastructure, including hospitals, primary care, and preventive health services.
The sector encompassing manufacturing, retail, wholesale trade, and commercial services.
The sector covering telecommunications, digital infrastructure, and information technology, including hardware, software, and connectivity systems.

The military sector is the part of a country’s economy and government responsible for producing, organizing, and maintaining armed forces and defense capabilities, including personnel, equipment, operations, and infrastrucutre.
The sector encompassing government agencies, civil services, and public institutions responsible for policy-making, regulation, and the delivery of public services in the context of climate change.
The sector providing social safety nets, welfare services, and support systems that protect vulnerable populations from economic and social risks.
The sector covering road, rail, air, and maritime transport systems, including infrastructure, vehicles, and logistics operations.
The sector responsible for water supply, sewage treatment, and solid waste management.
Non-profit organisations, advocacy groups, and community-based organisations that represent public interests, support communities, and hold governments and businesses accountable.
National, regional, and local government bodies responsible for setting policy, enacting legislation, and implementing programmes within their jurisdictions.
Individual people and domestic units whose everyday choices, behaviours, and circumstances make them both agents of and subjects of wider social and environmental change.
Commercial enterprises, industries, and business associations whose operations, investments, and innovations shape economic and environmental outcomes.
Supranational bodies including United Nations agencies, multilateral development banks, and intergovernmental organisations that coordinate policy, financing, and action across nations.
The highest level of governance, encompassing worldwide institutions, agreements, and processes that operate across all nations.

Governance arrangements and interventions involving a defined group of countries acting together across national boundaries, such as bilateral partnerships or plurilateral coalitions, without necessarily sharing a geographic region or formal institutional structure.
Governance operating at a regional geographic scale spanning multiple countries within a formally defined geographic or institutional bloc, such as the European Union or the African Union.
Governance and policy implemented at the level of a single sovereign nation, including national legislation, strategic plans, and government-led programmes.
Governance at the local or municipal level, including city councils and district authorities responsible for planning, service delivery, and local policy implementation.
Governance at the level of regions or provinces within a single country, such as states, counties, or devolved administrations with defined policy responsibilities.
The smallest unit of governance scale, referring to decisions and actions taken by individual people or households.
Formal urban settlements with a population of between 100,000 and 1,000,000 inhabitants, with established administrative systems, diverse economies, and relatively comprehensive urban infrastructure.
Formal urban settlements with a population exceeding 10,000,000 inhabitants, presenting unique challenges for governance, infrastructure, environmental management, and health system capacity.
Formal urban settlements with a population of between 1,000,000 and 10,000,000 inhabitants, characterised by complex governance structures, significant economic output, and high population density.
Formal urban settlements with a population of fewer than 100,000 inhabitants, typically characterised by local administrative functions, mixed economies, and partial urban service provision.

Planned, officially recognised urban areas with functioning administrative systems, legal land tenure, and access to infrastructure and services, categorised by population size following Revi et al. (2025).

Settlements established to house populations forcibly displaced by conflict, persecution, or disaster, including formal refugee camps, informal displaced person settlements, and spontaneous settlements in host communities. Distinct from other informal settlements in their governance structures, legal frameworks, humanitarian actors, and policy context, and complementary to concepts of forced displacement and migration by capturing the physical and administrative character of where displaced people live rather than the movement itself.

Dense informal urban settlements characterised by substandard housing, insecure tenure, limited access to clean water and sanitation, overcrowding, and social marginalisation, known by varied local names including favelas, bidonvilles, katchi abadis, and shanty towns.

Informal settlements not classified as slums, favelas, or refugee and displaced settlements, including other forms of unplanned or unauthorised housing such as illegal subdivisions, informal extensions of formal areas, and transitional settlements.

Residential areas characterised by lack of secure land tenure, inadequate infrastructure, poor access to basic services such as water, sanitation, and healthcare, and overcrowding. This category is intentionally broad, encompassing the diverse forms of unplanned or unauthorised settlement that develop on the periphery of formal cities, without relying on contested administrative labels that vary by country.

Areas at the urban-rural interface characterised by mixed land use, rapid demographic and physical change, and often partial or transitional access to urban services. The term is used variably across research traditions to describe either the rural-urban fringe of a growing city or areas that are administratively rural but functionally urban.

Africa is the world's second-largest continent by area and population, comprising 54 sovereign countries on a single landmass connected to Asia via the Sinai Peninsula, bordered by the Mediterranean Sea, Atlantic Ocean, Indian Ocean, and Red Sea.

Countries classified by the World Bank as having the highest gross national income per capita, generally with the greatest adaptive capacity but also the highest historical contributions to cumulative emissions.
Countries classified by the World Bank as having the lowest gross national income per capita, typically facing the greatest climate vulnerability and least adaptive capacity.
Countries classified by the World Bank in the lower-middle income tier, often experiencing rapid development while remaining highly vulnerable to climate-related health and economic impacts.
Countries classified by the World Bank in the upper-middle income tier, with growing capacity for climate adaptation and mitigation but still facing significant climate risks.
Regions characterised by low and variable rainfall, high evapotranspiration, and limited soil moisture, encompassing deserts, steppes, and dry shrublands where water scarcity is a primary constraint.

The world's largest terrestrial biome, spanning high-latitude northern regions and characterised by coniferous forest, cold winters, and short growing seasons, playing a major role in global carbon storage.
Shallow marine ecosystems built by calcium carbonate-secreting corals, supporting exceptional biodiversity and coastal protection but highly vulnerable to ocean warming and acidification.

Low-lying landforms formed by sediment deposition at river mouths or along river corridors, characterised by high agricultural productivity and biodiversity but acute vulnerability to flooding, sea-level rise, and storm surge.
Arid landscapes receiving very low annual precipitation, characterised by sparse vegetation and high temperatures, making them particularly vulnerable to heat stress and water scarcity.
Land used for agricultural production including arable crops, pasture, and mixed farming systems, representing a key interface between environmental conditions and food security.

Land covered predominantly by trees and associated flora, providing critical ecosystem services including carbon sequestration, biodiversity habitat, and water regulation, all threatened by climate change.
Inland water bodies including rivers, lakes, and streams, whose temperature, flow, and quality are sensitive to climate variability with consequences for drinking water and aquatic health.

Open landscapes dominated by grasses and low vegetation, sensitive to changes in precipitation and temperature, and at increased risk of drought and wildfire under climate change. Includes savanna (dominant in sub-Saharan Africa).
Land masses surrounded by water, particularly small island developing states, which face existential threats from sea level rise, coastal erosion, and increased storm intensity.

Coastal forest ecosystems dominated by salt-tolerant trees growing in intertidal zones of tropical and subtropical coastlines, providing habitat, carbon storage, and protection against storm surge and coastal erosion.

A climate zone and biome characterised by hot dry summers and mild wet winters, occurring around the Mediterranean Basin and analogous regions, with distinctive shrubland vegetation and high biodiversity.
Elevated terrain characterised by steep slopes and cooler temperatures, where glacier retreat, altered precipitation patterns, and biodiversity shifts are prominent climate change impacts.
Areas where land meets the sea, including coastlines, estuaries, and marine environments, highly exposed to sea level rise, storm surges, and ocean warming.

The transitional zone at the interface between urban and rural areas, characterised by mixed land use, rapid development, and populations that may lack full access to urban services while facing environmental pressures from adjacent cities.
Cold, high-latitude environments at the Earth's poles, experiencing some of the fastest rates of climate warming globally, with consequences for sea ice, permafrost, and global sea levels.
Dense tropical forests characterised by high biodiversity and rainfall, playing a critical role in global carbon cycling and increasingly threatened by deforestation and drought.

The transitional zone between terrestrial and aquatic environments along the banks of rivers, streams, and other watercourses, characterised by distinctive vegetation and sensitivity to flooding and drought.
Sparsely populated areas outside urban centres, often reliant on agriculture and natural resources, and facing distinct climate risks including drought, flooding, and reduced service access.
Regions located between the tropics and temperate zones, characterised by warm temperatures year-round, variable rainfall, and a mix of humid and dry subtropical climates.
Regions with moderate climates experiencing distinct seasons, where climate change is altering seasonal patterns, increasing extreme weather frequency, and affecting biodiversity.
Regions near the equator characterised by warm temperatures and high humidity year-round, where climate change is intensifying heat stress, vector-borne disease risk, and extreme rainfall.
A treeless biome found at high latitudes and elevations, characterised by permafrost, low vegetation, and extreme cold, with particular sensitivity to warming temperatures and permafrost thaw.
Densely populated areas characterised by built infrastructure and high human activity, where urban heat island effects and air pollution amplify climate-related health risks.
Low-lying areas between hills or mountains, often fertile and densely settled, which can be highly exposed to flooding and temperature extremes under climate change.
Low-lying ecosystems saturated with water, including marshes, swamps, and peatlands, which serve as important carbon stores and biodiversity habitats, threatened by drainage and climate change.
Exposure to outdoor or indoor air containing pollutants — including particulate matter, ozone, nitrogen dioxide, and wildfire smoke — at concentrations harmful to health.
Acute exposure to extreme meteorological events — including floods, storms, cyclones, droughts, and wildfires — that cause direct physical harm or injury.
Disruptions or changes to the availability, accessibility, and safety of food, including impacts on nutrition, foodborne pathogen risk, and agricultural productivity.
Physiological strain placed on the body by elevated ambient temperature and humidity, impairing thermoregulation and increasing the risk of heat-related illness.
Exposure to substandard, unsafe, or overcrowded living conditions that increase susceptibility to infectious disease, injury, and mental ill-health.
Economic disruption resulting in the loss of employment, income, or livelihoods, with downstream effects on food security, mental health, and access to healthcare.

pref_label: Loss of place attachment / cultural identity (Exposure)
definition: Psychological and social harm arising from disruption to a sense of belonging, cultural heritage, and connection to land or community — particularly relevant to indigenous and displaced populations.
Involuntary or forced movement of populations away from their homes due to environmental, conflict, or economic pressures, with associated health and social consequences.
Exposure to interpersonal or collective violence, including armed conflict, gender-based violence, and civil unrest, as a determinant of physical and mental health outcomes.
Social, economic, and structural conditions that mediate vulnerability to environmental hazards and shape health outcomes at individual and population level.
Exposure to ultraviolet radiation from solar sources, associated with skin cancer risk, vitamin D synthesis, and immune modulation.
Changes in the geographic range, abundance, and seasonal activity of vectors — such as mosquitoes, ticks and mites — that alter the transmission risk of vector-borne diseases.
Changes in the availability, quality, and safety of freshwater and other water sources, including flooding, drought, and contamination affecting drinking water and sanitation.
The rate of death from any cause within a defined population over a specified period, regardless of the underlying cause.
The rate of death attributable to a specific disease, condition, or cause within a defined population.
Deaths occurring earlier than expected relative to a baseline or reference population, or in excess of background mortality rates during a defined period or event.
Mortality rates among infants and children, typically measured as deaths per live births within specified age bands including neonatal, infant, and under-five periods.
The death of a woman during pregnancy, childbirth, or within 42 days of delivery from causes related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management.
A measure of premature mortality calculated as the years of life lost due to death before a defined life expectancy threshold.
Metrics quantifying fatal health outcomes, including overall and cause-specific death rates across populations.
A summary measure of population health combining years of life lost to premature death (YLL) and years lived with disability (YLD), representing the total burden of disease.
Self-reported or assessed measures of physical, mental, and social functioning and wellbeing as affected by a health condition or its treatment.
The rate at which new cases of a disease or condition occur in a defined population during a specified time period.
The proportion of a defined population living with a disease or condition at a specific point in time or during a defined period.
A component of the Global Burden of Disease framework measuring the years of healthy life lost due to living with a non-fatal disease or disability, weighted by severity.
Measures quantifying the non-fatal impact of disease on individuals and populations, including disease frequency, duration, and effect on functional status and wellbeing.
The proportion of disease cases or deaths in a population attributable to a specific exposure, estimating the potential reduction in burden if the exposure were eliminated.
Statistical measures comparing the probability of a health outcome between exposed and unexposed groups, used to quantify the strength of association between an exposure and an outcome.
Metrics that quantify the magnitude of an exposure or the proportion of outcomes attributable to that exposure in a defined population.
The rate or number of attendances at emergency departments for acute assessment and treatment, used as an indicator of urgent health need.
Interruptions to the availability or accessibility of healthcare services, resulting in delayed, reduced, or foregone care for affected populations.
The rate or number of patients admitted to hospital as inpatients for treatment, observation, or care related to a specific condition.
The duration of an inpatient hospital episode, used as a measure of disease severity, healthcare resource use, and patient recovery.
The rate or number of non-emergency contacts with primary care or outpatient services, including general practice, specialist clinics, and community health settings.
Metrics quantifying the use of healthcare services, including primary, secondary, and emergency care, as indicators of health system demand and population health need.
Deaths attributable to enteric infections transmitted via contaminated food or water, including diarrhoeal diseases and typhoid.

pref_label: Neglected tropical diseases and malaria mortality
definition: Deaths caused by neglected tropical diseases and malaria, disproportionately affecting populations in low-income tropical settings.
Deaths from infectious diseases not classified under respiratory, enteric, or vector-borne categories, including meningitis, encephalitis, and vaccine-preventable infections.
Deaths caused by infections of the respiratory tract, including tuberculosis, pneumonia, and other lower and upper respiratory infections.
Deaths caused by infectious and parasitic diseases, including respiratory, enteric, vector-borne, and other infections.
Deaths among women during pregnancy, childbirth, or the postpartum period attributable to obstetric causes.
Deaths occurring in the first 28 days of life, attributable to preterm birth, birth asphyxia, neonatal infection, and congenital conditions.
Deaths attributable to nutritional deficiencies and undernutrition, including protein-energy malnutrition and micronutrient deficiency disorders.

pref_label: Communicable, maternal, neonatal, and nutritional mortality
definition: Deaths attributable to communicable diseases, maternal conditions, neonatal disorders, and nutritional deficiencies.
Deaths attributable to diseases of the heart and circulatory system, including ischemic heart disease, stroke, and heart failure.
Deaths attributable to chronic conditions of the respiratory tract, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma.
Deaths attributable to diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease, which frequently co-occur and share common risk pathways.

pref_label: Injury-related mortality (drowning, fires, disasters, suicide, violence)
definition: Deaths resulting from injuries including drowning, fires, natural disasters, suicide, and interpersonal violence.
Deaths attributable to malignant and benign neoplasms across all anatomical sites.
Deaths attributable to non-communicable diseases not classified under the major NCD categories of cardiovascular, respiratory, neoplastic, or metabolic disease.
Deaths attributable to non-communicable diseases, including cardiovascular, respiratory, metabolic, and neoplastic conditions.
Deaths from any cause combined, used as an overall measure of fatal burden without attribution to a specific disease or condition.
The occurrence of death as a health outcome, classified by cause, age group, and population to characterise the fatal burden of disease.
An acute diarrhoeal illness caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, typically transmitted through contaminated water and capable of causing rapid dehydration and death.
Illness characterised by loose or watery stools, caused by a range of enteric pathogens and strongly associated with unsafe water, poor sanitation, and food contamination.
Severe systemic infection caused by non-typhoidal Salmonella serovars invading the bloodstream, predominantly affecting young children and immunocompromised individuals in low-income settings.
Systemic bacterial infections caused by Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Paratyphi, transmitted via contaminated food and water.
Intestinal infectious diseases not classified under diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid, or iNTS, including other bacterial, viral, and parasitic gut infections.
Infections of the gastrointestinal tract transmitted via contaminated food or water, including diarrhoeal diseases, typhoid, and cholera.
Infection caused by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which progressively damages the immune system and, without treatment, leads to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
Infections transmitted primarily through sexual contact, excluding HIV, including syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, and other sexually transmitted pathogens.
Infections transmitted through sexual contact or blood-borne routes, including HIV/AIDS and bacterial and viral sexually transmitted infections.
The spontaneous or induced termination of pregnancy before viability, including miscarriage, unsafe abortion, and related complications.
Medical conditions and complications directly related to pregnancy and childbirth, including haemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, obstructed labour, and sepsis.
Birth weight below 2,500 grams, associated with increased neonatal mortality, infection susceptibility, and long-term developmental and metabolic risk.
Birth occurring before 37 completed weeks of gestation, associated with increased risk of respiratory distress, infection, neurodevelopmental impairment, and neonatal death.
Conditions originating in the perinatal period affecting newborns, including preterm birth, birth asphyxia, neonatal infections, and congenital anomalies.
Conditions arising during pregnancy, childbirth, or the neonatal period, including obstetric complications and disorders of the newborn.
A vector-borne parasitic disease caused by Trypanosoma brucei, transmitted by tsetse flies, causing progressive neurological deterioration if untreated.
A vector-borne parasitic disease caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by triatomine bugs and endemic to Latin America, with chronic cardiac and digestive complications.
A mosquito-borne viral disease transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, causing acute fever and severe joint pain that can persist for months.
A zoonotic parasitic disease caused by the larval stage of Echinococcus granulosus tapeworm, producing fluid-filled cysts predominantly in the liver and lungs.
Infection by the larval stage of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium, which can invade the brain causing neurocysticercosis, a leading cause of acquired epilepsy.
A mosquito-borne viral infection caused by dengue virus serotypes, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, producing fever, severe headache, and in severe cases haemorrhagic complications.
A severe and often fatal viral haemorrhagic fever caused by Ebola virus, characterised by fever, bleeding, and multi-organ failure.
Parasitic infections caused by trematode flatworms acquired through consumption of contaminated raw or undercooked fish, crustaceans, or aquatic plants.
A parasitic infection caused by Dracunculus medinensis, acquired by drinking water containing infected copepods, resulting in a slowly emerging worm through the skin.
Parasitic worm infections transmitted through soil contaminated with faecal matter, including ascariasis, hookworm, and trichuriasis, causing malnutrition and developmental impairment.
A parasitic disease caused by Leishmania species, transmitted by sandflies, presenting as cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral forms.
A chronic bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae, affecting the skin, peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes, and historically associated with significant stigma.
A bacterial zoonosis caused by Leptospira species, transmitted through contact with water or soil contaminated by infected animal urine, with risk elevated during flooding events.
A mosquito-transmitted parasitic disease caused by filarial worms, leading to lymphatic damage, lymphoedema, and disfiguring swelling of the limbs and genitals.
A parasitic disease transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, caused by Plasmodium species, producing fever, anaemia, and potentially fatal cerebral complications.
A parasitic disease caused by Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by blackflies near fast-flowing rivers, causing skin disease and progressive visual impairment leading to blindness.
A fatal viral encephalitis caused by lyssavirus, transmitted through the bite of infected animals, almost universally fatal once clinical symptoms develop.
A parasitic disease caused by Schistosoma flatworms, transmitted through contact with contaminated freshwater, causing chronic inflammation of the bladder, liver, and intestines.
A chronic bacterial eye infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, the leading infectious cause of preventable blindness worldwide.
An acute viral haemorrhagic disease transmitted by Aedes and Haemagogus mosquitoes, endemic in tropical Africa and South America.
A mosquito-borne viral infection caused by Zika virus, typically mild in adults but associated with congenital microcephaly and Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Neglected tropical diseases not classified under specific GBD sub-categories, including other parasitic and bacterial infections endemic to tropical regions.
A diverse group of infectious diseases that disproportionately affect populations in tropical and subtropical low-income settings, including parasitic, bacterial, and viral conditions.

Growth faltering in children due to chronic undernutrition (stunting: low height-for-age) or acute undernutrition (wasting: low weight-for-height), with serious consequences for development and survival.
Insufficient dietary iron intake leading to iron deficiency anaemia, impairing oxygen transport, cognitive development, and immune function.
Conditions resulting from insufficient dietary iodine, including goitre, hypothyroidism, and cretinism, with adverse effects on thyroid function and neurodevelopment.
Severe deficiency of protein and energy intake, manifesting as marasmus (energy deficiency) or kwashiorkor (protein deficiency), predominantly affecting young children in food-insecure settings.
Deficiency of vitamin A resulting in night blindness, increased susceptibility to infection, and xerophthalmia, predominantly affecting children and pregnant women.
Nutritional deficiency conditions not elsewhere classified, including deficiencies in zinc, folate, calcium, and other micronutrients essential for health.
Conditions arising from insufficient intake of macro- or micronutrients, including protein-energy malnutrition and deficiencies in key vitamins and minerals.
Respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, ranging from mild infection to severe pneumonia, acute respiratory distress, and multi-organ failure.
Infections of the lower respiratory tract including the lungs and bronchi, such as pneumonia and bronchiolitis, representing a leading cause of morbidity and mortality.
Infection and inflammation of the middle ear, commonly caused by bacterial or viral pathogens following upper respiratory infection.
A chronic bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, primarily affecting the lungs but capable of affecting any organ system.
Infections of the upper respiratory tract including the nose, throat, sinuses, and larynx, typically caused by viruses.
Acute and chronic infections of the respiratory tract, including tuberculosis, pneumonia, and upper respiratory infections.
Acute inflammatory liver disease caused by hepatitis A, B, C, D, or E viruses, ranging from self-limiting illness to fulminant hepatic failure.

A vaccine-preventable bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, producing a toxin that causes a characteristic pharyngeal membrane and life-threatening airway obstruction and cardiac complications.
Inflammation of the brain parenchyma caused by viral, bacterial, or autoimmune processes, presenting with altered consciousness, seizures, and focal neurological signs.
A tick-borne bacterial infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, presenting with a characteristic expanding rash and potentially causing cardiac, neurological, and joint complications if untreated.
A highly contagious viral infection caused by measles morbillivirus, preventable by vaccination and causing fever, rash, and serious complications including pneumonia and encephalitis.
Inflammation of the meninges caused by bacterial, viral, or fungal pathogens, presenting with fever, headache, and neck stiffness and potentially fatal if untreated.
A highly contagious bacterial respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, characterised by severe paroxysmal coughing and particularly dangerous in infants.
A bacterial infection caused by Clostridium tetani toxin, producing painful muscle spasms and rigidity, with neonatal tetanus a particular risk in low-income settings.
Infection caused by varicella-zoster virus, producing chickenpox on primary infection and reactivating as herpes zoster (shingles) in older or immunocompromised individuals.
Infectious diseases not elsewhere classified, including rare, emerging, or unspecified infections not captured in major GBD sub-categories.
Infectious diseases not classified under respiratory, enteric, or vector-borne categories, including bacterial, viral, and prion conditions of diverse transmission routes.

pref_label: N.3.2 Communicable, maternal, neonatal, and nutritional diseases
definition: The broad category of diseases caused by infectious agents or related to maternal, neonatal, and nutritional conditions, as defined in the GBD cause hierarchy.
Pathological dilation of the aortic wall with risk of rupture, most commonly involving the abdominal aorta and associated with hypertension and atherosclerosis.
Cardiac arrhythmias characterised by rapid and irregular electrical activity in the atria, associated with stroke risk and heart failure.
Diseases of the heart muscle including cardiomyopathy and inflammation of the myocardium, leading to impaired cardiac function and heart failure.
Infection of the endocardium, most commonly involving the heart valves, caused by bacterial or fungal organisms and associated with significant morbidity and mortality.
Structural and functional cardiac disease caused by chronic elevation of blood pressure, leading to left ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure.
Reduction in blood supply to the heart muscle due to atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries, presenting as angina, myocardial infarction, or sudden cardiac death.
Atherosclerotic obstruction of the arteries supplying the lower limbs, causing claudication, ischaemia, and risk of amputation.
Dysfunction of one or more heart valves not attributable to rheumatic disease, including aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, and degenerative valve conditions.
Elevated blood pressure in the pulmonary arterial circulation leading to progressive right heart failure and exercise limitation.
Cardiac valve damage resulting from repeated episodes of rheumatic fever caused by group A streptococcal throat infection, predominantly affecting children and young adults in low-income settings.
Sudden interruption or rupture of blood supply to the brain, causing focal neurological deficits, classified as ischaemic or haemorrhagic in type.
Cardiovascular and circulatory diseases not elsewhere classified in the GBD framework, including peripheral vascular conditions and miscellaneous cardiac disorders.
Diseases of the heart and blood vessels, including ischemic heart disease, stroke, heart failure, and other circulatory conditions.
Allergic inflammation of the nasal mucosa triggered by inhaled allergens including pollen, dust mites, and moulds, causing sneezing, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhoea.
A chronic inflammatory airway disease characterised by reversible bronchoconstriction, wheeze, and airway hyperresponsiveness, triggered by allergens, pollutants, and respiratory infections.
A progressive, non-reversible obstructive lung disease characterised by persistent airflow limitation, associated with tobacco smoke, indoor and outdoor air pollution, and occupational exposures.

pref_label: Interstitial lung disease and pulmonary sarcoidosis
definition: A heterogeneous group of diffuse parenchymal lung diseases characterised by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung interstitium, leading to progressive breathlessness and impaired gas exchange.
Occupational lung diseases caused by chronic inhalation of mineral or organic dusts, including silicosis, coal workers pneumoconiosis, and asbestosis.
Chronic respiratory diseases not captured under the specific GBD sub-categories of COPD, pneumoconiosis, asthma, or interstitial lung disease.
Long-term diseases affecting the airways and lung parenchyma, including obstructive, restrictive, and inflammatory conditions causing progressive respiratory impairment.
Acute inflammatory disease of the glomeruli, typically immune-mediated, presenting with haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, and impaired renal function.
A group of metabolic diseases characterised by chronic hyperglycaemia resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both, with long-term damage to multiple organ systems.
Sudden deterioration of kidney function over hours to days, causing accumulation of waste products and fluid imbalance, often associated with sepsis, dehydration, or nephrotoxic exposure.
Irreversible, progressive loss of kidney function over months to years, classified by stages of declining GFR and associated with cardiovascular risk and need for renal replacement therapy.
Impaired kidney function assessed by reduced glomerular filtration rate or markers of renal damage, encompassing both chronic and acute kidney conditions.
A GBD grouping encompassing diabetes mellitus and kidney diseases, which share common metabolic risk factors and frequently co-occur.
Acute inflammation of the appendix, presenting with right iliac fossa pain and requiring surgical intervention to prevent perforation and peritonitis.

pref_label: Cirrhosis and other chronic liver diseases
definition: Progressive scarring and fibrosis of the liver resulting from chronic injury, including viral hepatitis, alcohol use, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, ultimately causing liver failure.
Conditions affecting the gallbladder and bile ducts, including cholelithiasis, cholecystitis, and biliary obstruction.
Chronic immune-mediated inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract, including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, characterised by relapsing intestinal inflammation.
Protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakness in the abdominal wall, including inguinal, femoral, and other hernias requiring surgical repair.
Acute or chronic inflammation of the pancreas, causing abdominal pain and disrupting digestive enzyme and insulin secretion.
Mechanical or functional obstruction of the intestine causing failure of intestinal transit, presenting with pain, distension, and vomiting.
Diseases affecting the oesophagus, stomach, and duodenum, including peptic ulcer disease, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and gastritis.
Conditions arising from impaired blood supply to the intestinal wall, including mesenteric ischaemia and ischaemic colitis.
Digestive diseases not classified under the specific GBD sub-categories of liver, upper GI, appendix, hernia, IBD, vascular, gallbladder, or pancreatic disease.
Non-infectious diseases of the gastrointestinal tract and related organs, including the liver, gallbladder, and pancreas.
A group of mental disorders characterised by excessive fear or worry disproportionate to circumstances, including generalised anxiety disorder, panic disorder, and phobias.
A neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by persistent inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that impairs functioning across multiple settings.
A neurodevelopmental condition characterised by persistent difficulties in social communication and interaction alongside restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour.
A mood disorder characterised by episodes of mania or hypomania alternating with depression, causing significant disruption to functioning and quality of life.
A disruptive behavioural disorder characterised by repetitive and persistent patterns of antisocial behaviour, aggression, or violation of social norms.
A common mental disorder characterised by persistent low mood, anhedonia, and a range of cognitive, physical, and emotional symptoms causing significant functional impairment.
Mental disorders characterised by abnormal eating behaviours and distorted body image, including anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge eating disorder.
Significantly impaired intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour arising from neurodevelopmental causes, without an identifiable acquired or genetic aetiology.
A trauma- and stressor-related disorder developing after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, characterised by intrusive symptoms, avoidance, and hyperarousal.
A severe chronic mental disorder characterised by positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions), negative symptoms (blunted affect, social withdrawal), and cognitive impairment.
Mental disorders not classified under the major GBD mental health sub-categories, including other anxiety, dissociative, somatic, and unspecified psychiatric conditions.
Conditions characterised by clinically significant disturbances in cognition, emotion regulation, or behaviour, reflecting dysfunction in psychological or biological processes.
Diseases of bones, joints, muscles, and connective tissue, including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, osteoporosis, and low back and neck pain.
A malignant tumour arising from melanocytes in the skin, strongly associated with ultraviolet radiation exposure and with high metastatic potential.
Malignant tumours arising from keratinocytes in the skin, including basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, associated with cumulative UV radiation exposure.
Malignant tumours arising in the trachea, bronchi, or lung parenchyma, strongly associated with tobacco smoking and air pollution exposure.
Malignant neoplasms not classified under the specific GBD cancer sub-categories, spanning other primary tumour sites and histological types.
Non-malignant tumours that do not invade surrounding tissue or metastasise but may cause local symptoms through mass effect.
Diseases characterised by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells, including malignant cancers and benign tumours across all anatomical sites.
Progressive neurodegenerative diseases characterised by cognitive decline, including Alzheimer's disease and other dementias causing loss of memory, reasoning, and functional independence.
Chronic neurological disorders characterised by recurrent headache, including migraine, tension-type headache, and cluster headache, causing significant disability.
A neurological disorder characterised by recurrent unprovoked seizures due to abnormal electrical activity in the brain, not attributable to an identified structural or metabolic cause.
A progressive neurodegenerative disease causing degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, leading to progressive paralysis and respiratory failure.
A chronic autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, characterised by relapsing or progressive neurological deficits affecting motor, sensory, and cognitive function.
A progressive neurodegenerative disease characterised by tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability, caused by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra.
Neurological conditions not classified under the major GBD neurological sub-categories, including rare and unspecified disorders of the nervous system.
Diseases affecting the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nervous system, including degenerative, inflammatory, and functional neurological conditions.
Partial or complete loss of hearing attributable to ageing, noise exposure, ototoxic medications, or other causes, affecting communication and quality of life.
A spectrum of visual impairment ranging from reduced vision to complete blindness, caused by refractive errors, cataracts, glaucoma, macular degeneration, and infectious causes including trachoma.
Sense organ diseases not classified under blindness and vision loss or hearing loss, including other ocular and otological conditions.
Diseases affecting the organs of vision and hearing, including conditions causing visual impairment, blindness, and hearing loss.
A chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit characterised by comedones, papules, pustules, and nodules, predominantly affecting the face and trunk.
An autoimmune condition causing patchy non-scarring hair loss on the scalp or other hair-bearing areas, which may progress to total hair loss.
Bacterial infections of the skin and soft tissue, including cellulitis, impetigo, and erysipelas, caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes.
Localised skin and underlying tissue injury resulting from prolonged pressure or shear forces, typically over bony prominences in immobile patients.
Inflammatory skin conditions characterised by erythema, pruritus, and scaling, including atopic dermatitis and contact dermatitis.
Skin infections caused by fungi including dermatophytes (tinea), yeasts (candidiasis), and moulds, particularly prevalent in hot and humid conditions.
A chronic or recurrent sensation of itching without a primary skin lesion, often associated with systemic disease, dry skin, or neuropathic conditions.
A chronic immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease characterised by scaly erythematous plaques, with systemic associations including psoriatic arthritis.
